title: The Church
lead: The community of those who belong to Christ. The Greek word ekklesia means an assembly called together, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel gathered before the LORD. In the New Testament it names a house group, a city's believers, and the whole people of God, pictured as a body, a building, a bride and a household.

sections.b: In everyday Greek an ekklesia was the citizens' assembly of a city. The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, uses it for the Hebrew qahal, Israel gathered at Sinai or before the king (Deuteronomy 9:10; 1 Kings 8:14). Jesus uses the word only twice in the Gospels, both in Matthew (Matthew 16:18; 18:17). Paul writes to the church of God in Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:2) and also speaks of one church of God that he once persecuted (Galatians 1:13).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 9:10; Matthew 16:18; Matthew 18:17; 1 Corinthians 1:2; Galatians 1:13; Acts 19:32

sections.b: Paul and his school draw four pictures of the church. A body with Christ as head and many parts (Romans 12:4-5; 1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 1:22-23; Ephesians 4:11-16). A building or temple with Christ as cornerstone (1 Corinthians 3:9-17; Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:4-8). A bride (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25-32; Revelation 21:2). A household or family (Galatians 6:10; Ephesians 2:19; 1 Timothy 3:15). The churches differ on how visible, how ordered and how united the church must be; the cards on Ephesians 2:20 and Ephesians 4:4-6 set them side by side.
sections.refs: Romans 12:4-5; 1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 1:22-23; Ephesians 2:19-22; Ephesians 5:25-32; 1 Peter 2:4-8; Revelation 21:2
